title: July/August 2026
gist: This record is the table of contents of Foreign Affairs Volume 105, Number 4 (July/August 2026), not a single essay — it lists titles, subtitles and authors only. As an attention map it shows the US foreign-policy establishment's agenda tilting overwhelmingly to military-technological disruption and the collapse of nuclear deterrence, a split verdict on Chinese power, the Middle East after the Iran war, and one dedicated essay on AI-driven domestic political crisis.

insights.claim: Paul Scharre argues in the July/August 2026 Foreign Affairs that new technologies threaten America's military advantage, framed as the United States 'losing the war of the future'.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: Establishment consensus is shifting toward US military-technical vulnerability — supportive of sustained defence-innovation and autonomy budgets over legacy platforms.
insights.quote: Losing the War of the Future How New Technologies Threaten America’s Military Advantage Paul Scharre

insights.claim: Rose Gottemoeller, writing on 'The Strange Defeat of Nuclear Deterrence', argues a crisis in strategic stability is coming.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: A former arms-control negotiator forecasting deterrence breakdown raises tail risk for nuclear-adjacent escalation and for arms-control-linked policy trades.
insights.quote: The Strange Defeat of Nuclear Deterrence And the Coming Crisis in Strategic Stability Rose Gottemoeller

insights.claim: Jennifer Lind and Daryl G. Press argue the American nuclear umbrella is broken and ask what replaces extended deterrence for US allies.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: Direct input to allied proliferation risk in Asia and Europe — watch Japan, South Korea and Germany nuclear-latency debates.
insights.quote: The Broken Nuclear Umbrella What Comes After Extended Deterrence Jennifer Lind and Daryl G. Press

insights.claim: Of the twelve lead essays in the July/August 2026 issue, eight concern military power, deterrence or war, and only one concerns economics-adjacent technology disruption — an agenda weighted to hard security rather than trade or finance.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: Attention-allocation signal: the US policy elite is budgeting mindshare to conflict scenarios, which historically precedes defence-spending and export-control expansion.

insights.claim: Dennis Blair argues China's military edge is a mirage and that American panic about it is both misguided and counterproductive.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: A named contrarian case against the China-threat consensus; if it gains traction it caps the political ceiling for China-driven defence escalation.
insights.quote: The Mirage of China’s Military Edge Panic Is Misguided—and Counterproductive Dennis Blair

insights.claim: Ely Ratner and Nick Danby argue China's power contains exploitable fault lines and that America must both build and actively use leverage against Beijing.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: Signals continued bipartisan appetite for coercive economic tools against China regardless of administration.
insights.quote: The Fault Lines in China’s Power America Must Build—and Use—Leverage Against Beijing Ely Ratner and Nick Danby

insights.claim: Patricia M. Kim argues a 'China First' transactional foreign policy will fail, drawing lessons about the limits of transactionalism.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: Frames Beijing's own dealmaking as structurally limited — relevant to durability of Chinese bilateral commodity and infrastructure deals.
insights.quote: Why “China First” Will Fail The Limits and Lessons of a Transactional Foreign Policy Patricia M. Kim

insights.claim: Ian Johnson argues Beijing is suffering a self-inflicted identity crisis, posing the question 'Who Is China?'
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: Domestic legitimacy strain is being treated as a live variable in Chinese behaviour, not just external constraint.
insights.quote: Who Is China? Beijing’s Self-Inflicted Identity Crisis Ian Johnson

themes.theme: Middle East after the Iran war

insights.claim: Dana Stroul argues the Iran war will transform America's military role in the Middle East, describing a regional 'power paradox'.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: US force posture in the Gulf is being repriced — relevant to Gulf sovereign risk premia, shipping insurance and regional defence procurement.
insights.quote: The Middle East Power Paradox How the Iran War Will Transform America’s Military Role Dana Stroul

insights.claim: Narges Bajoghli and Vali Nasr argue a remade Islamic Republic has adopted a new grand strategy that will reshape the Middle East.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: Iran is being modelled as reconstituted rather than defeated — argues against pricing a durable post-war calm in energy and freight.
insights.quote: Iran’s New Grand Strategy How a Remade Islamic Republic Will Reshape the Middle East Narges Bajoghli and Vali Nasr

themes.theme: Russia, forever wars and the next order

insights.claim: Michael Kofman argues Moscow's military power after the Ukraine war constitutes 'the next Russia threat' rather than a spent force.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: Underpins sustained European rearmament demand even in a Ukraine-ceasefire scenario.
insights.quote: The Next Russia Threat Moscow’s Military Power After Ukraine Michael Kofman

insights.claim: Michael Beckley and Hal Brands frame the coming contest for global order as 'Heartland vs Rimland' — a geographic bloc division rather than a bilateral US-China rivalry.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: A usable mental model for bloc formation: expect trade and technology alignment to sort along continental-versus-maritime lines.
insights.quote: Heartland vs. Rimland The Battle Lines in the War for the Next Global Order Michael Beckley and Hal Brands

insights.claim: Carter Malkasian argues the costs of collective forgetting about Afghanistan and the forever wars remain unreckoned in US strategy.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: Institutional memory loss is being flagged as a driver of repeat intervention risk.
insights.quote: The Afghanistan Reckoning Forever Wars and the Costs of Collective Forgetting Carter Malkasian

themes.theme: AI shock and domestic political risk

insights.claim: James A. Davidson and Matthew J. Slaughter present a policy playbook explicitly aimed at averting a political crisis caused by the AI shock, treating AI labour disruption as a governance emergency rather than a productivity story.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: AI political backlash is now on the establishment policy agenda — front-run regulatory and redistribution responses that could hit AI adopters' labour economics.
insights.quote: How to Survive the AI Shock A Policy Playbook to Avert Political Crisis James A. Davidson and Matthew J. Slaughter

insights.claim: Sheri Berman argues American democracy is a broken system in need of structural repair, in an essay titled 'A Democracy Safe for the World'.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: Domestic institutional fragility is treated as a foreign-policy variable, raising the discount on US policy predictability.
insights.quote: A Democracy Safe for the World How to Fix a Broken System Sheri Berman

insights.claim: Zachariah Mampilly argues US policy toward Africa is misconceived and will get worse before it gets better.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: Reinforces the vacuum thesis in Africa that Chinese and Gulf capital have been filling.
insights.quote: Why America Gets Africa Wrong U.S. Policy Will Get Worse Before It Gets Better Zachariah Mampilly

insights.claim: The issue's debate sections give dedicated space to whether Europe should fear a more powerful Berlin and to competing approaches to Pyongyang, signalling both are treated as unsettled questions rather than settled policy.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: German rearmament and Korean-peninsula policy are contested — expect volatility in both files rather than a stable trend.
insights.quote: The German Question Should Europe Fear Berlin? Hanns W. Maull; Liana Fix
